Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Wang et al. generated conditional CBP/p300 double KO in alpha-cells on alpha-cell expansion and mass, differentiation and function. Pancreatic alpha-cell-specific deletion of CBP/p300 induced hypoglucagonemia and hyperaminoacidemia, without affecting fasting blood glucose. Alpha-cell CBP/p300 dKO impaired postnatal alpha-cell expansion and differentiation, resulting in decreased alpha-cell mass and to development of hypoglucagonemia. In addition, CBP/p300 deficiency prevented glucagon receptor antibody-stimulated alpha-cell proliferation. Mechanistically, the authors describe a novel CBP/p300-Slc7A2 axis, regulating lysine-induced histone acetylation, including that of the glucagon (Gcg), Mafb and Pcsk2 genes. CBP/p300 KO induces autophagic cell death through attenuation of SLC7A2/arginine-stimulated mTORC1 signaling. Collectively, the authors conclude that in alpha-cells, CBP/p300 are central regulators of alpha-cell mass and function by orchestrating SLC7A2-mediated amino acid sensing. In general, the study design is sound, the findings are interesting, and the manuscript is well-written. However, CBP and p300 are ubiquitous nuclear proteins that play a central role in regulating histone acetyl-transferase activity; therefore, it is not surprising that knocking out both genes impair transcription and cellular growth, differentiation and function. The role of this pathway in regulating alpha-cell function in physiology, e.g. under conditions of amino acid deprivation or overload is not clear. It is also not clear whether this pathway is perturbed in diabetes and/or obesity. New experimental data are required to strengthen the core mechanistic components of the proposed model and to demonstrate its relevance to disease pathophysiology.
Major Comments
1. Are there any alterations in CBP, p300 and/or Slc7a2 expression in alpha-cells in animal models of diabetes and/or obesity/metabolic associated liver dysfuncton(MASLD) and even more important in human subjects? Of note, alpha-cell dysfunction was present only under conditions of complete ablation of both CBP and p300, suggesting that the activity of these proteins is partially redundant and dispensable, therefore it is unlikely that partial inhibition of these genes in obesity or diabetes (if exist) is sufficient to induce alpha-cell dysfunction, arguing against the suggestion that this pathway is involved in disease pathophysiology.
Response: This is a very good question. To directly address this issue, we first examined whether CBP, p300, or Slc7a2 expression is altered in α cells under diabetic or obese conditions. Single-cell RNA sequencing data and immunofluorescence staining revealed comparable gene and protein expression intensities of CBP, p300, and Slc7a2 in the α cell of db/db mice, high-fat diet (HFD)-fed mice, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) human islets compared to corresponding controls (Extended Data Fig.3a, 3e-j). Similarly, no significant alterations in the expression of CBP, p300, or Slc7a2 were observed at either the mRNA or protein level in bulk islets from T2DM patients (Extended Data Fig.3b-d), according to human islet data from HumanIslets.com [8]. These results indicate that the expressions of CBP, p300, and Slc7a2 in α-cell are preserved across metabolic disease states and pathogenic activation of this pathway is unlikely to arise from altered gene abundance alone. Rather, our α cell-specific CBP/p300 knockout model illuminates that this signaling module is nutrient-responsive, pointing toward substrate-driven activation as the more plausible mechanism in metabolic diseases. Supporting this interpretation, our previous work in the 4C cohort, a large-scale human metabolomic study demonstrated a strong correlation of 2-aminoadipic acid (2-AAA), a catabolite of lysine, with the incidence of type 2 diabetes [9]. In our separate study, we further showed that 2-AAA promoted hepatic gluconeogenesis through CBP/p300-mediated transcriptional activation of gluconeogenic genes [10]. Therefore, it is likely that excessive amino acid flux stimulates α cell hyperfunction through intact CBP/p300-SLC7A2 axis, contributing to the subsequent elevation of blood glucose.

2. Glucagon deficiency affected amino acids degradation, but not hepatic glucose production, evident by similar fasting glucose, pyruvate tolerance and expression of gluconeogenic enzymes. Are mouse models of glucagon deficiency relevant for studying the role of glucagon in human physiology? Please explain.
Response: Thank you for highlighting this important point. Although glucagon is well known for its rapid glucose-elevating action and clinical use in treating severe hypoglycemia, we did not observe decreased fasting glucose level in CBP/p300αDKO mice despite their hypoglucagonemia. Similar findings have been reported in other models: (i) α-cell ablation using diphtheria toxin in embryos or adult mice minimally affects fasting glucose [11-13], and (ii) Gcg knockout mice also maintain normal fasting glucose levels [14]. These findings suggest that basal hepatic glucose production can be preserved through residual glucagon secretion and compensatory mechanisms that maintain glucose homeostasis. In contrast, amino acid dysregulation is a highly penetrant and conserved hallmark of glucagon deficiency. Elevated circulating amino acid levels have been consistently observed in Gcg knockout, Gcgr knockout, and GCGR antibody blockade mouse models [15]. Li Hong et al. reported a patient with a homozygous GCGR c.958_960del (p.Phe320del) variant who exhibited normal blood glucose level, but persistent hyperaminoacidemia [16]. Patients undergoing pancreatectomy likewise develop severe hyperaminoacidemia that can be alleviated by glucagon administration, whereas individuals with glucagon-producing tumors exhibit profound hypoaminoacidemia [17]. A practical extension of this conserved biology is that plasma amino acid concentrations are now used clinically as pharmacodynamic readouts of GCGR activity in trials of dual (glucagon/GLP-1) or triple (glucagon/GLP-1/GIP) receptor agonists [18].
3. The authors argue that SLC7A2/arginine, rather than SLC38A5/glutamine regulates mTORC1 and autophagy. Previous studies showed that GCGR antagonism induces alpha-cell proliferation through glutamine transport via SLC38A5, thereby stimulating mTORC1. The authors found that the expression of both Slc7a2 and Slc38a5 decreased in CBP/p300 dKO mice. They should add control experiments of Slc38a5 knockdown and/or over-expression and study the effects on mTORC1 activity and autophagy in alpha-cells to convincingly show that the SLC7A2 transporter is indeed the main regulator of mTORC1-autophagy signaling in alpha-cells. The authors over-expressed Slc7a2 in islets and claim that this enhanced arginine stimulation of mTORC1 (Fig. 7d). This statement is not entirely supported by the data: Slc7a2 over-expression increased mTORC1 activity in absence of arginine, while the response to arginine was in fact abrogated. Fig. 7b-e lack quantifications, and the number of repeated experiments is not mentioned, therefore it is difficult to interpret the findings.
Response: We thank you for this excellent and important comment. Our single-cell RNA sequencing analysis revealed that Slc7a2 exhibited high and widespread expression across nearly all WT pancreatic α cells, whereas Slc38a5 was expressed only in a small subset of α cells and at much lower levels (Extended Data Fig.4a-c), consistent with prior studies [2, 13, 19]. Moreover, in α-cell-specific Slc38a5 knockout mice, reduced α-cell proliferation and mass are observed only under GCGR blockade, with no alterations under physiological conditions [2]. Given the robust and ubiquitous expression of Slc7a2 in α cells and the limited prior research, we therefore focused our investigation on this transporter. Although Slc38a5 expression was also reduced in the knockout mice, its low basal expression suggests it is unlikely to be the major contributor under normal conditions; however, a potential auxiliary role cannot be ruled out. We have revised this part in discussion.
Regarding Fig.7d, a careful review of our experimental records revealed a possibility that the use of DMEM medium led to basal mTORC1 activation in the Slc7a2-overexpressing cells even without additional arginine stimulation. To eliminate this confounding factor, we repeated the experiment using amino acid-free HBSS prior to arginine treatment. Under these corrected conditions, Slc7a2 overexpression clearly enhanced arginine-induced mTORC1 activation (Revised Fig.7d). We sincerely thank you for highlighting this issue. Quantifications for Figure 7b-e (based on n=3 independent experiments) have been incorporated to Supplementary Fig.7a-d.

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
Wang et al. use Gcg-Cre to delete the histone acetyltransferases p300 and CBP in pancreatic α cells. The KO shows a partial reduction in circulating glucagon and modest increases in several plasma amino acids, which the authors attribute to loss of α cell identity, reduced α cell mass and proliferation, arising from diminished α-cell gene expression. They nominate Slc7a2 as a mediator, and that the reduced Slc7a2 leads to reduced H3K27Ac at the Gcg and Mafb loci and their gene downregulation, and a failure to mount α-cell hyperplasia after anti-Gcgr treatment.
The findings on α-cell identity and proliferation overlap with prior Neurog3-Cre genetics showing that p300/CBP are required for islet endocrine cell mass and proliferation. Please cite and discuss this study, since the overlap limits the incremental advance. A significant issue is that most data shown are underpowered, with experiments from Figures 1c, 2, 3, 5, and 6 presented at n = 3 and no justification of sample size.
For the core narrative, the authors argue that loss of p300/CBP downregulates Slc7a2, which then maintains α-cell identity through H3K27Ac at Gcg and Mafb, and amino acid-driven proliferation. This interpretation does not fully acknowledge that p300/CBP are fundamental drivers of tissue-specific gene expression that establish endocrine identity. It is therefore equally plausible that Slc7a2 downregulation is a downstream consequence of identity erosion rather than the primary cause. To support causality, one would need in vivo evidence that Slc7a2 loss is sufficient to reduce H3K27Ac at Gcg and Mafb with concordant transcriptional downregulation. A recent Slc7a2-/- report does not show loss of α-cell identity. For proliferation, α cells lacking p300/CBP already show impaired proliferation, so the lack of an amino acid response may reflect a general failure to traverse the cell cycle, in addition to any defect in amino acid sensing.
Response: We appreciate your detailed review and valuable suggestions, which have been instrumental in improving the quality of our paper. In the revised manuscript, we cite and discuss the Neurog3-Cre study. Mice lacking all four copies of p300/CBP in pancreatic endocrine progenitors failed to establish ɑ- and β-cell mass postnatally. This innovative study reveals the pivotal role of p300/CBP in pancreatic islet development and provide valuable insights for our research, yet notable differences exist between the studies. Firstly, the referenced study utilized the Ngn3-Cre line, which targets endocrine progenitors during pancreatic development. As Ngn3 expression peaks during embryogenesis (E9.5–E15.5), this model is well-suited for investigating islet cell differentiation and development. Ngn3-Cre-mediated p300/CBP knockout occurs prior to pancreatic α-cell formation, potentially impacting α-cell development. In contrast, our study employed Gcg-Cre to specifically target glucagon-expressing α-cells, focusing on the role of p300/CBP in these cells. Additionally, we used Gcg-CreERT mice to examine the effect of p300/CBP on mature α-cells. Secondly, the Ngn3-Cre model displayed glucose homeostasis dysregulation due to impaired β-cell function and mass, with limited exploration of p300/CBP’s role in α-cells. In the study of Wong et al., Ngn3-Cre-driven pancreatic islet-specific p300 knockout mice displayed reduced proliferation of neonatal α-cells and β-cells. Mice lacking all copies of p300/CBP died postnatally, which prevents further investigation. In our study, the expansion and maintenance of postnatal α cell number were normal in single-gene knockout (CBPαKO, p300αKO) or triple-allele knockout (CBPαKO; p300HE, CBPHE; p300αKO) mice, while α-cell numbers were unchanged at postnatal day 0 (P0) in CBP/p300αDKO mice, with a decline in proliferation observed postnatally. Furthermore, GCGR blockade did not induce α-cell hyperplasia. Using lineage-tracing mice, α-cell specific double knockout of CBP/p300 led to loss of α-cell identity and increased cell death, further highlighting distinct mechanisms in our model compared to the Ngn3-Cre-based approach. Sample sizes were increased to 4-5 per group according to your suggestion.
Our in vivo and in vitro experiments identified CBP and p300 as the critical regulators of α cell identity, autophagy, and proliferation. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed a high and widespread expression of Slc7a2 in WT pancreatic α cells and significant downregulation in CBP/p300αDKO α cells. Further in vitro experiments demonstrated the effect of CBP/p300 on Slc7a2 expression and the vital role of Slc7a2 in regulating α cell identity and autophagy-related gene expressions. Moreover, overexpression of Slc7a2 could partially rescue the reduced proliferation caused by CBP/p300 deficiency in α cells. As a result, it is reasonable to suppose that CBP/p300-SLC7A2 axis is critical for the expansion and maintenance of functional pancreatic α cell mass.
We agree that p300/CBP loss likely causes broad disruptions in cell cycle regulation, given their role in orchestrating transcriptional programs. However, our study specifically highlights the diminished proliferative response to amino acid stimulation in p300/CBP-deficient α-cells, which correlates with Slc7a2 downregulation. This observation suggests that Slc7a2-mediated amino acid signaling is a critical component of the proliferative defect. Supporting this, our GCGR blockade model failed to induce α-cell hyperplasia, consistent with impaired amino acid-driven proliferation in the absence of p300/CBP. We are grateful for your critical insights, which prompts us to refine our interpretations and design targeted follow-up experiments to strengthen our conclusions.

Response: Thank you for your constructive criticism. Based on your comment, we performed ex-vivo glucagon secretion assays in islets isolated from WT and CBP/p300αDKO mice. Glucagon secretion was reduced in islets of CBP/p300αDKO mice in response to arginine (Extended Data Fig.22a), indicating that CBP/p300 deficiency compromises α-cell function. We treated α-TC1-6 cells with another well-known CBP/p300-HAT inhibitor C646 and the specific CBP/p300-bromodomain inhibitor, I-CBP112. Like A-485, C646 significantly suppressed the expression of functional genes in α cells. (Mol Metab2024) demonstrated the increase of non-alpha cells (mainly delta or beta cells) in a Slc7a2-mTORC1 dependent manner, while in this study, Ppy-positive glucagon cells were increased. In the referenced study, alpha cell hyperplasia and increased proliferation rates of beta and delta cells were both observed in the different models of interrupted glucagon signaling. Extended Data Fig. 35. Pathway enrichment profiles of α-cell subpopulations based on GSVA analysis. (a) GSVA heatmap showing enrichment scores of selected GO biological processes across the four α-cell subpopulations. (b) Glucagon secretion from isolated islets of WT or CBP/p300αDKO mice in response to 1 mM glucose (1G), 5 mM glucose (5G) or 5G + 10 mM Arginine (Arg) (n = 3). Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Statistical significance was determined using two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test. Compared with WT group: **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001. (Supplementary Fig.4)
5) The transcriptional regulation of Slc7a2 is of great significance. However, it is not clear whether CBP/p300 directly regulate transcription of Slc7a2. Please demonstrate the CBP/p300 location on the promoter/enhancer sites of Slc7a2 genes, and their absence in the DKO mice.

We analyzed H3K27Ac ChIP-seq and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) data of mouse pancreatic islets and related cell lines using the ChIP-Atlas database [21]. We sincerely thank the editor and all reviewers for reviewing our revised manuscript and providing detailed feedback. Below, we provide a detailed point-by-point response to all comments. Newly added data are included in the revised figures and text as indicated.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
1. A major missing link in the proposed model is the claim that loss of p300/CBP downregulates Slc7a2 as a key mechanistic step, as implied by the title (“CBP/p300-Slc7a2 axis is critical for the expansion and maintenance of functional pancreatic α cell mass”). This is crucial to demonstrate because p300/CBP broadly regulates cell type-specific transcription; therefore, the loss of α-cell mass/identity cannot be attributed specifically to Slc7a2 downregulation. Moreover, Slc7a2 downregulation in the p300/CBP knockout is unlikely to be a major driver of the phenotype, given that p300/CBP HAT inhibitors have a much stronger effect on α-cell gene transcription than Slc7a2 silencing (Figure 5). The authors should explicitly discuss that Slc7a2 is unlikely to be the primary mechanism linking p300/CBP loss to the α-cell phenotypes and revise the “axis/through” framing accordingly.
Response: We sincerely thank you for your thoughtful comments. Indeed, CBP/p300 deficiency induces profound alterations in the epigenome and transcriptome in pancreatic α-cells of CBP/p300αDKO mice. Slc7a2 is unlikely to be a dominator of the process. However, Slc7a2 downregulation is, at least in part, involved in this phenotype. Following your suggestions, we added this discussion and revised corresponding descriptions to avoid overstatement.
2. If the authors wish to retain some claims of a direct p300/CBP-Slc7a2 axis, the current revision does not provide locus-level evidence to support this. Because p300/CBP recruitment is typically indirect, formaldehyde-only ChIP may be insufficient to assess occupancy. Supportive experiments would include (i) p300/CBP ChIP using a longer-range crosslinker (e.g., EGS) at the Slc7a2 locus, or (ii) ChIP-qPCR for H3K27ac at the Slc7a2 locus after manipulating p300/CBP activity. These would strengthen the locus-level association, though they would still not fully distinguish direct effects from indirect consequences of altered α-cell identity programs from loss of p300/CBP.
Response: Thank you for this constructive feedback. To address your concerns, we treated α-TC1-6 cells with the selective p300/CBP HAT inhibitor A-485 and performed ChIP-qPCR for H3K27ac at the Slc7a2 promoter. As shown below, A-485 treatment significantly reduced H3K27ac enrichment at the Slc7a2 promoter region (Extended Data Fig.1a). Moreover, our previous H3K27Ac ChIP-seq data from A-485-treated rat islets showed similar changes (Extended Data Fig.1b). While indirect recruitment via α-cell lineage TFs likely mediates initial p300/CBP localization, our results highlight the essential role of their acetyltransferase function in locus activation and α-cell maturation. To avoid overstatement, we deleted the description of p300/CBP-Slc7a2 axis according to your suggestion.

Green rectangles indicate regions with significantly reduced H3K27Ac enrichment upon A-485 treatment. Data are presented as mean ± SEM. Statistical significance was determined using two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test. **P < 0.01. (Fig.5k and Supplementary Fig. 5e)
3. Line 999 (“Fig. 6 Knockout of CBP/p300 triggers α cell autophagy through SLC7A2/arginine-regulated mTORC1 signaling”). The data support that CBP/p300 knockout and Slc7a2 silencing can each trigger α-cell autophagy, but do not establish that CBP/p300 loss induces autophagy through Slc7a2. Please revise the figure title and related text to avoid implying causality between the two.
Response: We appreciate your valuable and insightful critique. As suggested, we revised the title of Figure 6 to avoid a causal relationship.
4. The authors should discuss non-histone acetylation as a plausible contributor to α-cell regulation, given the broad effects of CBP/p300 perturbation.
Response: Good suggestion! We added this relevant discussion in our revised manuscript.
5. Line 101, revise to “oral glucose tolerance test” for clarity.
Response: As suggested, we revised the description in the new version.
6. The claim that loss of p300/CBP leads to cell death remains unaddressed (e.g., lines 440-441, 897 etc). The authors should revisit these statements and rephrase them precisely as cell loss/reduced α-cell mass.
Response: We appreciate your valuable suggestion. We have carefully revised all relevant statements throughout the manuscript to replace "cell death" with precise terminology.
Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
The revised manuscript was modified according to the reviewers’ comments including mine, and has been improved significantly. My major concerns about the origin and the “healthiness” of the alpha cells of each subgroup have been well taken and discussed. I have only minor comment related to the previous points.
I think the discussion on the identity of glucagon cells in the DKO was quite essential, and the information on the expression of disallowed genes in the authors’ responses was very important. It should be noted that the highly differentiated alpha cells exhibited not only amino acid-induced glucagon secretion but also glucose-suppressed glucagon secretion, which is a marked difference from beta cells. Now that the authors included the data on glucagon secretion in response to glucose in the revised manuscript, I wonder if the authors can add information on the expression of the genes related to glucose responsiveness (Glucose transporters, Gck, Abcc8, Kir6.2 and others). I also suggest that these data should be combined with Extended data Fig34 and be briefly mentioned in the text with Supplemental data.
Response: We sincerely thank you for the time and effort dedicated to reviewing our manuscript with the thoughtful and constructive comments, which have been instrumental in improving the quality of our work. As suggested, we added the new data on glucose-responsive gene expressions to Supplementary Fig. 4b and updated the text accordingly.

Violin plots displaying absolute expression levels of islets progenitor, β-cell identity and α-cell glucose-responsive genes across GCG, Both, tdTomato, and NONE groups. (Supplementary Fig. 4b)

You are a senior editor at Nature Communications.

Read the paper and the peer-review interaction below. Based on the scientific concerns raised by the reviewers and the authors' point-by-point response, predict the editorial outcome.

Respond with EXACTLY one of these labels on the first line:
  major_revision
  minor_revision
  accept

Then provide a 2–3 sentence rationale explaining your prediction.

## Paper

## Abstract

Pancreatic α cell senses amino acid availability to adjust secretion function and proliferation, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, α cell-specific deletion of CBP/p300 in mice leads to hypoglucagonemia and hyperaminoacidemia, along with decreased functional pancreatic α cell mass due to impaired cell proliferation, dedifferentiation, and cell loss. The knockout of CBP/p300 blocks glucagon receptor antibody-stimulated α cell proliferation and mTORC1 signaling in mice. In CBP/p300 deficient α cells, single-cell RNA sequencing reveals upregulated autophagy-related genes and downregulated α cell identity genes and amino acid transporters, including Slc7a2. Slc7a2 is involved in regulating α cell identity gene expression through lysine-facilitated H3K27 acetylation. In addition, Slc7a2 downregulation compromises arginine-stimulated mTORC1 signaling, thereby suppressing α cell proliferation and triggering autophagy. Collectively, our findings uncover CBP/p300 as central regulators of functional α cell mass partially by orchestrating Slc7a2-mediated amino acid sensing.

---

## Introduction

As structural elements and energy sources for normal cell growth and function, amino acids are essential to human health1. The disturbance of amino acid homeostasis has been closely linked to metabolic diseases. Branched-chain amino acids and their metabolites have been identified as the strongest biomarkers of obesity, insulin resistance, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM)2. 2-Aminoadipic acid (2-AAA), a catabolic metabolite of lysine, could even predict the risk of developing T2DM3. It is widely recognized that impaired pancreatic β-cell function is the core problem in T2DM4. However, accumulating evidence suggests that α cell dysfunction, characterized by inappropriate glucagon secretion, also contributes to hyperglycemia in diabetes5. Notably, α cell function and number is tightly coupled to changes in plasma amino acid levels6. However, the response mechanism of α cells to amino acids remains largely unclear.

Pancreatic α cells are essential to maintaining glucose homeostasis primarily through secreting glucagon, which promotes hepatic glucose production during fasting or hypoglycemic states7. Glucagon binds to the glucagon receptor (GCGR), activating PKA-CREB signaling cascades that stimulate hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis8. In addition, glucagon facilitates hepatic amino acid uptake and catabolism, thereby supplying substrates for glucose production9. Thus, glucagon secreted from α cell plays a critical role in the turnover of amino acids to glucose in hepatocytes, resulting in decreased circulating amino acid concentration and increased blood glucose level. In turn, changes in plasma glucose and amino acid levels modulate glucagon secretion in an opposite direction6. In T2DM, α cell dysregulation is characterized by excessive basal glucagon secretion that occurs independent of glycemic status, contributing to hyperglucagonemia and increased hepatic glucose output10,11.

Recent studies have highlighted the role of α cells as key amino acid sensors12. In humans, the ingestion of whey protein induces a significant rise in circulating amino acids and glucagon levels13. Several amino acids, including arginine, glutamine, alanine, and glycine, have been shown to acutely stimulate glucagon secretion14. Prolonged elevations of amino acids also drive excessive α cell proliferation, leading to its hyperplasia and hyperglucagonemia15-18. Increased circulating glutamine has been shown to be causative to amino acid-induced α cell hyperplasia in GCGR signaling interference models, involving the upregulation of SLC38A5, a transporter of glutamine, and stimulation of mTORC1 pathway. However, whether or how α cells sense other types of amino acids, especially those related to T2DM, remains elusive.

It has been demonstrated that amino acids provide substrates for several protein post-translational modifications such as acetylation and crotonylation, which link amino acids catabolism to the transcriptional regulation of genes involved in cell function or proliferation19,20. Besides cell number, the maintenance of α cell identity is also critical for their function21,22. Epigenetics plays a crucial role in the maintenance of cell type-specific features and lineage stability22,23. ATAC-Seq analysis shows that α cells possess more poised and accessible chromatin at genes related to identity and diabetes risk22. Histone acetylation is an important epigenetic modification involved in regulating cell type-specific gene expression patterns and determining cell fate24. The lysine acetyltransferases type 3 (KAT3) family members CBP (Crebbp) and p300 (Ep300) are key transcriptional co-activators with similar structure and function23. Of interest, acetylation of H3 lysine 27 (H3K27Ac) mediated by CBP and p300 is reported to be a biomarker of cell type-specific promoters and enhancers related to cell fate25. However, the role of CBP/p300 in controlling α cell identity remains poorly under stood.

In this study, we generated α cell-specific Crebbp/Ep300 knockout mice to explore the role of two acetyltransferases in maintaining α cell identity. Dual deletion of CBP and p300 led to a significant reduction in functional α cell mass and glucagon secretion due to impaired α cell proliferation, α cell dedifferentiation, and cell loss. Single-cell RNA sequencing and in-vitro experiments revealed the involvement of SLC7A2 in CBP/p300-governed α cell identity, proliferation, and autophagy through lysine-promoted histone H3K27 acetylation and arginine-stimulated mTORC1 activation. These findings uncover a critical role for CBP/p300 in linking amino acid sensing with the maintenance of α cell identity and function.

---

## Results

Pancreatic α cell-specific double knockout of Crebbp and Ep300 mice exhibit low plasma glucagon level and high amino acid level

To investigate the role of CBP and p300 in pancreatic α cells, we generated α cell-specific CBP/p300 knockout (CBP/p300αDKO) mice by crossing Gcg-Cre mice with Crebbpflox/flox and Ep300flox/flox mice (Fig. 1a). The knockdown efficiency was confirmed by immunofluorescence staining within 1 day after birth, showing negative CBP and p300 staining in more than 90% Gcg-positive α cells of CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 1b, c). The potential off-target effects of Gcg-Cre in intestinal L-cells and brain were also evaluated. Intestinal co-expression of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and tdTomato in Gcg-Cre-driven tdTomato lineage-tracing wild-type (WT) and CBP/p300αDKO mice confirmed that Gcg-Cre was indeed active in the intestinal L-cells (Supplementary Fig. 1a). However, neither the average number of GLP-1+ cell per intestinal section nor circulating level of active GLP-1 differed between control and CBP/p300αDKO mice (Supplementary Fig. 1b, c). In addition, CBP/p300αDKO mice exhibited normal oral glucose tolerance (Supplementary Fig. 1d), further indicating preserved L-cell function. We also confirmed Gcg-Cre-mediated recombination in neurons of the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) (Supplementary Fig. 1e). The preproglucagon neurons of NTS have been reported to regulate appetite and energy metabolism26,27, but no significant alterations were observed in food intake or energy expenditure in CBP/p300αDKO mice (Supplementary Fig. 1f, g), suggesting minimal impact on the central nervous system.

Interestingly, fasting blood glucagon level was significantly reduced in 8-week-old CBP/p300αDKO mice, but not in single-gene knockout (CBLPαKO, p300αKO) or triple-allele knockout (CBPαKO; p300HE, CBPHE; p300αKO) mice compared to wild-type (WT) controls (Fig. 1d). However, fasting blood glucose and plasma insulin levels remained unchanged in 8-week-old CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Fig. 1h), accompanied by normal hepatic glucose output (Fig. 1f) and mRNA levels of key gluconeogenic genes, including Pck1, Fbp1, and G6pc (Fig. 1g). This was the case for the levels of PEPCK protein and phosphorylated CREB (Fig. 1h). In contrast, total plasma amino acid level was significantly increased in fasted CBP/p300αDKO mice compared to WT controls (Fig. 1i). We further performed metabolomic assays on plasma samples from 8-week-old WT and CBP/p300αDKO mice. A total of 193 metabolites were identified, with univariate analysis revealing 53 upregulated and 2 downregulated metabolites in CBP/p300αDKO mice (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1j). Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted that differential metabolites were mainly associated with amino acid metabolism, including arginine and proline metabolism, as well as alanine, aspartate, glutamate, glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism (Fig. 1k). Of the 20 basic amino acids examined, 16 were significantly increased, including several glucogenic amino acids such as alanine, glutamine, and serine (Fig. 1l). These results suggest that CBP and p300 deletion in α cells causes hypoglucagonemia and significant disturbance in amino acid homeostasis, without affecting plasma glucose levels.

CBP/p300 is necessary for the expansion and maintenance of postnatal α cell number

During murine islet endocrine cell development, glucagon (Gcg)-positive cells first appeared at embryonic day 9.528. We next examined whether CBP/p300 deletion-mediated hypoglucagonemia is due to impaired development or postnatal maintenance of Gcg-positive α cells. Morphometric analysis showed that Gcg-positive cell number in CBP/p300αDKO mice was normal at birth (0 w) (Fig. 2a, b, Supplementary Fig. 2a), indicating that CBP/p300 are not essential for α cell development. With the elongation of postnatal time, significant difference was observed in Gcg-positive cell number between WT and CBP/p300αDKO mice. In WT mice, α cell numbers increased rapidly during the first 2 weeks, with the fastest growth occurring between 1 and 2 weeks. Afterward, the rate of α cell expansion slowed and stabilized from 4 weeks onward (Fig. 2b). Whereas, α cell number was decrease by 37% at 2 weeks and 70% at 8 weeks in CBP/p300αDKO mice compared to WT mice (Fig. 2b, c). We further analyzed additional morphometric indicators. At 2 weeks, pancreatic weight and the average number of islets per section were similar between two groups (Supplementary Fig. 2b). However, the α cell area as a percentage of the total islet area was significantly reduced in CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 2d), with similar α cell size between two groups (Fig. 2e). Notably, the number of Gcg-positive α cells per islet was dramatically decreased in CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 2f), while the number of β, δ, and PP cells remained unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 2c).

We also examined α cell proliferation during the neonatal period, which plays a key role in postnatal α cell mass establishment29. Ki67 staining revealed a significant decrease in α cell proliferation in 1-week-old CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 2g, h), consistent with the reduced α cell expansion observed in these mice (Fig. 2i). However, the apoptosis rates of α cell were comparable in 4 and 8 week-old WT and CBP/p300αDKO mice as shown by cleaved-Caspase 3 staining (Supplementary Fig. 2d), indicating that other forms of cell loss may contribute to the decline in α-cell numbers. At 8 weeks, although pancreatic weight and the average number of islets per section were similar between WT and CBP/p300αDKO mice (Supplementary Fig. 2e), the α cell area as a percentage of total islet area was even further reduced in CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 2j), with no significant change in α cell size (Fig. 2k). The number of Gcg-positive α cells per islet remained significantly lower in CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 2l), while the β cell area was still unaffected (Supplementary Fig. 2f). Together, these results demonstrate that CBP/p300 are essential for the postnatal proliferation and survival of α cells.

Double deficiency of CBP and p300 leads to α-cell identity loss and population reduction

Building on our previous findings that HAT activity of CBP/p300 are critical for the transcription of β cell identity genes30, we next investigated their role in α cell fate maintenance using a lineage-tracing system based on ROSA-LSL-tdTomato reporter mice crossed with Gcg-Cre to label glucagon-expressing (Gcg+) α cells (Fig. 3a). The labeling efficiency was confirmed in 2-week-old ROSAfl/wt;Gcg-Cre mice, in which over 90% of Gcg+ cells co-expressed tdTomato (Supplementary Fig. S3a, b). We then examined islet sections at postnatal weeks 1, 2, 4, and 8, and found that nearly all tdTomato+ cells consistently co-expressed Gcg in WT mice (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Fig. 3c). However, CBP/p300αDKO mice showed a progressive and significant reduction in the number of tdTomato+ cells per islet section starting from 2 weeks of age (Fig. 3c), indicating tdTomato+ cell loss. Although the percentage of tdTomato+Gcg+/tdTomato+ cells in the knockout mice was similar to WT at 1 week, it dropped to 79% at 2 weeks, 55% at 4 weeks, and 32% at 8 weeks (Fig. 3d), indicating a gradual loss of α cell identity. Immunofluorescence staining revealed no significant transdifferentiation into β or δ cells in CBP/p300αDKO mice when α cell lost its identity. However, the ratio of tdTomato+Ppy+ cells was significantly reduced in CBP/p300αDKO mice compared to WT mice (Fig. 3e, f).

To further investigate the role of CBP/p300 in adult α cells, we generated tamoxifen-induced α cell-specific CBP/p300 knockout mice (iCBP/p300αDKO) by crossing Gcg-CreERT2 with Crebbpflox/flox/Ep300flox/flox mice, and ROSA-LSL-tdTomato reporter mice (Fig. 3g). Tamoxifen administration in 8-week-old mice resulted in efficient tdTomato labeling of Gcg+ cells (> 90%) (Fig. 3h, Supplementary Fig. 3d). In line with findings from CBP/p300αDKO mice, iCBP/p300αDKO mice exhibited decreased fasting plasma glucagon level and elevated plasma amino acid level, without changes in fasting blood glucose level (Supplementary Fig. 3e-g). Histological analysis revealed that iCBP/p300αDKO mice had significantly fewer tdTomato+ cells and Gcg+ α cells compared to WT mice (Fig. 3i, j), as well as a reduced proportion of tdTomato+Gcg+/tdTomato+ cells (Fig. 3k), further supporting the occurrence of α cell loss and dedifferentiation. Similar to the developmental model, no transdifferentiation of α cells into β or δ cells was observed, but tdTomato+ Ppy+ cells were also diminished (Fig. 3l, m). Together, these results confirm that CBP/p300 are indispensable for maintaining α cell survival and identity throughout the postnatal life.

Expressions of α cell identity genes are compromised in CBP/p300αDKO mice

To elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying α cell identity loss in CBP/p300αDKO mice, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on islet cells from 4-week-old WT and CBP/p300αDKO mice using tdTomato as a lineage tracer (Fig. 4a). Intact islets were isolated from two groups of mice, dissociated into single-cell suspensions, and subjected to scRNA-seq analysis. After filtering out low-quality cells and doublets, 11,797 high-quality cells, including 4,993 from WT mice and 6,804 from CBP/p300αDKO mice were retained for downstream analysis. Dimensionality reduction and clustering analysis identified seven major cell types, including β, α, δ, and PP cells, as well as acinar, endothelial, and immune cells, based on canonical markers (Fig. 4b, c). Lineage tracing showed that approximately 90% of Gcg+ cells in WT mice expressed tdTomato, validating efficient Cre recombination (Fig. 4d, e).

To characterize α-cell state transitions in the absence of CBP/p300, we performed pseudotime trajectory analysis on α cells from CBP/p300αDKO mice due to tdTomato marking biologically distinct α-cell states in WT versus CBP/p300αDKO mice, which would otherwise confound joint trajectory interference. The trajectory showed a temporal progression from tdTomato-negative (tdTomato-) to tdTomato-positive (tdTomato+) α cells, with tdTomato- cells mainly located at early to intermediate stages, while tdTomato+ cells enriched at intermediate to late stages, suggestive of a differentiation trajectory toward identity loss following Cre-mediated CBP/p300 deletion (Fig. 4f, g). Gene expression dynamics along pseudotime identified four co-regulated modules with temporal expression patterns, including a decline in α cell identity genes (e.g., Gcg, MafB, and Ttr) and a concurrent upregulation of autophagy-related genes (e.g., Ctsf, Ctsl, and Tmem59) (Fig. 4h). Consistent with the downregulation of α-cell identity genes, islets isolated from CBP/p300αDKO mice exhibited markedly impaired ex vivo glucagon secretion in response to basal glucose, low glucose, and arginine, indicating functional impairment of α cells following CBP/p300 ablation (Supplementary Fig. 4a).

We next investigated the transcriptional disruptions in α cells by performing UMAP co-visualization of Gcg and tdTomato expression in α cells from CBP/p300αDKO mice. This revealed two major tdTomato+ subsets. One retained high Gcg expression and another lacked Gcg expression, indicative of heterogeneous α cell states (Fig. 4i, j). Based on the expression levels of Gcg and tdTomato, four α cell subpopulations were defined: (i) Gcg+tdTomato+ cells (Both, 42%), representing functional α cells; (ii) Gcg- tdTomato+ cells (tdTomato, 39%), denoting identity-compromised α cells; (iii) Gcg+tdTomato- cells (GCG, 14%), likely α cells escaping recombination; and (iv) Gcg- tdTomato- cells (NONE, 5%), potentially immature α cells (Fig. 4k).

To further dissect molecular changes across these α cell subpopulations, we analyzed the expression of key markers associated with known markers, identity, autophagy, transdifferentiation, dedifferentiation, glucose-responsiveness and amino acid metabolism (Fig 4l, Supplementary Fig. 4b). Gcg and MafB expressions were diminished in the tdTomato group, confirming identity erosion. Autophagy-related genes, such as Map1lc3a, Map1lc3b, Lamp1, Lamp2, Atp6v0c and Ctsf, were upregulated in the tdTomato group, while the expressions of Ins1, Mafa and Ucn3 remained unchanged, excluding transdifferentiation into β cells. In the tdTomato group, Ngn3 was undetectable and other progenitor-related genes showed no significant changes, arguing against persistence of progenitor-like cells. Several glucose-responsive genes, such as Gck and G6pc2 were significantly downregulated in the tdTomato group. Notably, expressions of amino acid transporter genes (Slc16a10, Slc38a5, Slc38a4, and Slc7a2) were profoundly altered in identity-lost tdTomato group, implicating impaired amino acid sensing in the progression of α cell dysfunction.

SLC7A2 is involved in the regulation of α cell identity gene expression via lysine-facilitated histone acetylation modification

Based on the transcriptional disruptions observed in α cells of CBP/p300αDKO mice from scRNA-seq, we sought to identify key metabolic genes involved in the maintenance of α cell identity. Differential expression analysis highlighted Slc7a2, encoding a cationic amino acid transporter for lysine and arginine20,31, as one of the most significantly downregulated genes in α cells from CBP/p300αDKO mice compared to WT controls (Log2 Fold Change = -1.0578, P value = 1.0074E-140) (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Violin plots confirmed that this downregulation was specific to α cells, with minimal changes observed in other islet cell types (Fig. 5a). Pseudotime analysis revealed a progressive decline in Slc7a2 expression along the α cell differentiation trajectory in CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 5b). Correlation analysis further showed that Slc7a2 expression positively correlated with key α cell identity markers (Gcg, MafB, and Pcsk2) and negatively with autophagy-related genes (Ctsf and Ctsl) (Fig. 5c), suggesting a potential association with α cell dysfunction and stress responses. Immunofluorescence staining confirmed reduced SLC7A2 protein level (Fig. 5d, Supplementary Fig. 5b), accompanied by a significant decrease in MafB expression in α cells of CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 5e, Supplementary Fig. 5c).

CBP/p300 are known to regulate lineage-specific gene expression through histone H3K27 acetylation30,32. Consistent with this, H3K27Ac level was significantly reduced in α cells of CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 5f, Supplementary Fig. 5d). Structurally, CBP/p300 possess a histone acetyltransferase (HAT) domain that catalyzes acetylation of lysine residues and a bromodomain that recognizes acetylated lysines to facilitates chromatin targeting33. To determine the contribution of each domain to transcriptional regulation of α cell genes, we treated primary islets from WT mice with either I-CBP112 (a bromodomain inhibitor34, 5 μM) or A-485 (a selective HAT inhibitor35, 3 μM). Only A-485 markedly suppressed the expressions of Gcg, Mafb and Slc7a2 (Fig. 5g), highlighting the crucial role of CBP/p300 HAT activity in maintaining α cell identity. This was further validated in α-TC1-6 cells, where A-485 treatment led to similar decreases in the expressions of these genes (Fig. 5h). ChIP-qPCR analysis revealed that A-485 markedly lowered H3K27Ac enrichment at their promoter regions (Fig. 5i-k), a finding consistent with our previous H3K27Ac ChIP-seq data from A-485-treated rat islets (Supplementary Fig. 5e).

Amino acid metabolism has been implicated as a key regulator of α cell identity and function36. In this study, we found that amino acid starvation conditions (HBSS) significantly reduced the mRNA expressions of Gcg, MafB, Pcsk2, and Slc7a2 in α-TC1-6 cells (Fig. 5l). Similarly, Slc7a2 knockdown produced a similar effect, supporting the essential role of Slc7a2-mediated amino acid transport in maintaining α cell identity. On the contrary, lysine supplementation significantly upregulated the expression of these identity genes and partially rescued the inhibitory effects of Slc7a2 knockdown (Fig. 5m), suggesting that Slc7a2-mediated lysine uptake supports α cell function. Ex vivo islet secretion assays further demonstrated that lysine pretreatment enhanced both basal and arginine-stimulated glucagon secretion (Supplementary Fig. 5f). Mechanistically, lysine catabolism yields acetyl-CoA, which serves as a substrate for histone acetylation37. Supporting this, ChIP-qPCR analysis showed that lysine treatment significantly increased H3K27Ac levels at the promoters of Gcg and MafB (Fig. 5n, o). We further tested whether the catabolite of lysine 2-AAA, a known biomarker of T2DM, elicits similar effects. Indeed, 2-AAA treatment robustly elicited the expression of Gcg, Mafb, and Pcsk2 (Fig. 5p), with elevated H3K27Ac levels at their promoters (Fig. 5q, r), linking amino acid metabolism to CBP/p300-dependent epigenetic regulation of α cell identity genes.

Together, these results suggest that Slc7a2-mediated lysine uptake fuels acetyl-CoA production, thereby promoting CBP/p300-dependent histone acetylation and expression of α cell identity genes (Fig. 5s).

Both CBP/p300 inhibition and Slc7a2 silencing trigger amino acids-regulated α cell autophagy

Autophagy is essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis38. It is specifically activated in response to amino acid starvation through two key signaling cascades: the mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) and general control nonderepressible 2 (GCN2) pathway39,40. To assess autophagic activity in CBP/p300αDKO mice, we performed single-cell gene set enrichment analysis (scGSEA), which revealed significant upregulation of lysosome-related genes in α cells (Fig. 6a, b). Immunofluorescence staining showed a higher percentage of tdTomato+ α cells with LC3 puncta, a hallmark of autophagosome formation41, in knockout mice (Fig. 6c, d). Consistently, higher accumulation of autophagosomes was observed in α cells from CBP/p300αDKO mice compared to WT mice as shown by transmission electron microscopy (Fig. 6e, f, Supplementary Fig. 6a), confirming increased autophagic flux in the absence of CBP/p300.

To determine whether amino acid availability regulates autophagic activity in α cells, we treated α-TC1-6 cells with HBSS. This treatment significantly upregulated the mRNA expression of autophagy-related genes (Fig. 6g). Importantly, knockdown of Slc7a2 in α-TC1-6 cells also increased the expression of autophagy markers (Fig. 6h), suggesting that Slc7a2 modulates autophagic activity. CBP/p300 inhibition by A-485 elicited a similar response (Fig. 6i). Furthermore, Slc7a2 knockdown in α-TC1-6 cells led to elevated level of LC3-II, a marker of autophagosome accumulation (Fig. 6j, Supplementary Fig. 6b). This was the case for A-485 treatment (Fig. 6k, Supplementary Fig. 6c), further supporting the roles of Slc7a2 and CBP/p300 in amino acids-regulated autophagy.

CBP/p300 deficiency blocks glucagon receptor antibody-stimulated α cell proliferation

Arginine activates the mTORC1 signaling pathway to regulates cell growth and proliferation42. Since Slc7a2 mediates arginine uptake, it is reasonable to suppose that Slc7a2 influences α cell proliferation by activating mTORC1. To test this, isolated mouse islets were cultured with DMEM (control), HBSS (starvation), and arginine (Fig. 7a). Under starvation condition, mTORC1 activation in islets α-cells was significantly reduced as shown by low phosphorylation of S6 (pS6), a key downstream target of mTORC143. Conversely, arginine supplementation enhanced mTORC1 activation (Fig. 7b, Supplementary Fig. 7a). Slc7a2 knockdown blunted the ability of arginine to activate S6 phosphorylation in α-TC1-6 cells (Fig. 7c, Supplementary Fig. 7b), whereas Slc7a2 overexpression potentiated mTORC1 activation in response to arginine (Fig. 7d, Supplementary Fig. 7c), indicating that Slc7a2 is indeed a key arginine sensor in α cells. To examine whether CBP/p300 inhibition affects mTORC1 signaling through Slc7a2 regulation, we treated α-TC1-6 cells with A-485. This treatment significantly diminished arginine-stimulated mTORC1 activation (Fig. 7e, Supplementary Fig. 7d).

The link between hyperaminoacidemia and α cell proliferation has been well established in models with disrupted glucagon signaling44. To assess the impact of CBP/p300 loss on α cell responses to amino acids, WT and CBP/p300 knockout mice were treated with a monoclonal antibody (REMD 2.59) targeting GCGR (Fig. 7f). Immunofluorescence analysis showed that GCGR antibody treatment strongly increased the number of tdTomato+ α cells in WT mice, whereas this effect was abolished in CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 7g). Quantification confirmed a significant expansion of tdTomato+ cells per islet in WT mice following GCGR signaling blockade, without significant change in knockout mice (Fig. 7h). Proliferative activity was further assessed by co-staining for Ki67. In WT mice, GCGR mAb robustly increased the proportion of Ki67+ tdTomato+ α cells, while CBP/p300-deficient mice failed to mount a proliferative response (Fig. 7i), indicating that CBP/p300 are required for α cell proliferation in response to glucagon receptor inhibition. We next examined mTORC1 signaling by assessing phosphorylation of S6. GCGR antibody significantly increased the proportion of pS6⁺ tdTomato⁺ cells among tdTomato⁺ cells in WT islets, but this induction was markedly blunted in CBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 7j, k), indicating impaired mTORC1 activation.

To validate these findings in an inducible model, we administered GCGR antibody to iCBP/p300αDKO mice. Similarly, GCGR signaling blockade promoted α cell expansion in WT mice, but failed to increase tdTomato+ cell numbers in iCBP/p300αDKO mice (Fig. 7l, m). Ki67 staining also showed enhanced α cell proliferation in WT mice, but not in knockout mice (Fig. 7l, n). pS6 staining was significantly lower in iCBP/p300αDKO mice compared to WT controls (Fig. 7o, p). Collectively, these findings suggest that CBP/p300 are necessary for α cell proliferation and proper mTORC1 signaling in response to glucagon receptor blockage.

## Methods

Mice

Crebbp-Loxp (Crebbpflox/flox) and Ep300-Loxp (Ep300flox/flox) mice were generated by Gempharmatech CO. using the CRISP-Cas9 system to insert LoxP sites flanking exon 2 of the Crebbp or Ep300 genes. Gcg-Cre knock-in (Gcg-Cre) mice (Stock No. 030663) were acquired from the Jackson Laboratory, while Gcg-IRES-CreERT2 knock-in (Gcg-CreERT2) mice were generated via CRISPR-Cas9 by Gempharmatech CO. ROSA26-tdTomato reporter mice (Stock No. 007909) were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory. For generating conditional Crebbp and Ep300 knockout mice, Crebbp/Ep300flox/flox mice were crossed with Gcg-Cre mice. The resulting F1 progeny (Crebbpflox/wt/Ep300flox/wt; Gcg-cre) were interbred with Crebbpflox/wt/Ep300flox/wt mice. This breeding strategy yielded the following specific genotypes: Crebbpflox/flox/Ep300wt/wt; Gcg-cre (CBPαKO) mice, Crebbpwt/wt/Ep300flox/flox; Gcg-cre (p300αKO) mice, Crebbpflox/flox/Ep300flox/wt; Gcg-cre (CBPαKO/p300HE) mice, Crebbpflox/wt/Ep300flox/flox; Gcg-cre (CBPHE/p300αKO) mice and Crebbpflox/flox/Ep300flox/flox; Gcg-cre (CBP/p300αDKO) mice. Cre-negative littermates from each mating combination were used as wild-type (WT) controls. To generate inducible α-cell-specific Crebbp and Ep300 double knockout (iCBP/p300αDKO) mice, Gcg-CreERT2 mice were crossed with Crebbpflox/flox/Ep300flox/flox mice. For induction of Cre-mediated recombination, mice aged 6-8 weeks received three intraperitoneal injections of tamoxifen (Sigma-Aldrich #T5648) at 100 µg/g body weight, with each injection spaced 24 hours apart. For lineage tracing studies, ROSA26-tdTomato reporter mice were further bred with CBP/p300αDKO or iCBP/P300αDKO mice to facilitate tracking of Crebbp or Ep300 deletion in specific cells. Both male and female mice were used in this study. All mice were kept on a C57BL/6J background and housed under specific pathogen-free conditions, following a standard 12-hour light/dark cycle with unrestricted access to food (normal chow) and water. Animal protocols were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Shanghai Model Organisms Center, Inc., Shanghai, China.

Genomic PCR for mouse genotyping

Mouse genotype was detected with genomic DNA prepared from tail using One Step Mouse Genotyping Kit (Vazyme, PD101-01). Multiple pairs of primers were used to identify different genetic modifications. For Crebbp/Ep300 floxed alleles, Crebbp-F1/Crebbp-R1 and Ep300-F1/Ep300-R1 primer pairs were used. The Crebbp-F1 and Crebbp-R1 primers were used to distinguish WT (147bp) or floxed Crebbp allele (245bp), whereas the Ep300-F1 and Ep300-R1 primers were used to distinguish WT (416bp) or floxed Ep300 allele (521bp). For Cre recombinase detection, three different Cre systems were genotyped: Gcg-Cre was detected using Gcg-Cre-P1, Gcg-Cre-P2, and Gcg-Cre-P3 primers; Gcg:CreERT2 was identified using Gcg:CreERT2-F1 and Gcg:CreERT2-R1 primers; and Rosa26 reporter alleles were genotyped using Rosa-P1, Rosa-P2, Rosa-P3, and Rosa-P4 primers to distinguish between different Rosa26 allelic states. The primer sequences used for genotyping mice are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

Metabolic studies

Random and 16 h-fasting blood glucose concentrations were measured using a glucometer (Accu-Chek, Roche, Mannheim, Germany) by tail vein sampling. For pyruvate tolerance test, the mice in an overnight-fasting state received an i.p. injection of sodium pyruvate (2 g/kg body weight, Sigma Aldrich), blood glucose concentration was measured before and 15, 30, 60, and 120 min after pyruvate injection. Fasting plasma glucagon level was quantitated using homogenous time-resolved FRET (HTRF) assays (Cisbio/PerkinElmer). Fasting plasma insulin level was detected by mouse insulin Elisa kit (Mercodia). The level of total fasting plasma amino acids was measured using a commercially available Total Amino Acid assay kit (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute).

We performed the metabolomics analysis by Q300 Kit according to a detailed procedure (Metabo-Profile, Shanghai, China). A ultraperformance liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) system (ACQUITY UPLC-Xevo TQ-S, Waters Corp., Milford, MA, USA) was used to quantitate all targeted metabolites in this study by Metabo-Profile Biotechnology (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed. The volcano plot integrated the log2 (Fold Change) and P-value. VIP (variable importance in projection) was obtained based on the OPLS-DA model. Differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs) were selected with VIP ≥ 1 and P-value < 0.05. The Z-score indicates standard deviations concerning the mean of the control group. The raw data are provided in Supplementary Data 1.

For GCGR mAb treatments, the animals were treated weekly with 5 mg/kg of a humanized monoclonal anti-GCGR antibody (REMD 2.59) intraperitoneally for 4 weeks via intraperitoneal administration as previously reported67.

Immunofluorescence staining and image analysis

Mouse whole pancreas (including head, body, and tail) was dissected, fixed in 4% formalin and processed for paraffin embedding. For the immunostaining analysis, entire pancreatic tissues were continuously sectioned at 5-μm thickness. The primary antibodies were added and incubated overnight at 4 ℃. Then tissue sections were treated with fluorescence-labeled secondary antibody and stained with DAPI. For cell quantification in the immunofluorescent staining, six to eight equally spaced sections (which covered the entire pancreas) per pancreas were imaged using a TissueGnostics microscope or a ZEISS LSM880 confocal microscope, and the total numbers of positive staining cells from three to five mice per group were counted manually. The α cell area from the glucagon antibody-stained sections and β cell area from the insulin antibody-stained sections were measured using HistoQuest software (TissueGnostics).

Ex vivo islet assays

Mouse pancreatic islets were isolated as described in our previous study68. For amino acid starvation experiment, islets from 4 weeks old C57BL/6J mice were overnight recovered in RPMI-1640 containing 16.7 mM glucose and 10% FBS. They were then cultured in RPMI-1640 containing 16.7 mM glucose and 0.2% BSA or Hanks' balanced salt solution (HBSS) containing 16.7 mM glucose and 0.2% BSA for 50 min. For arginine re-stimulation experiment, starved islets were then stimulated with 400 μM arginine for 10 min. At the end of the culture, these islets were fixed in 4% formalin for 24 h and subsequently blocked in 1% agarose gel and embedded in paraffin. These islets paraffin blocks were continuously sectioned at 5-μm thickness. Then immunofluorescence staining was performed on the tissue section to detect the phosphorylated level of S6 in Gcg+ cells.

Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis

For the single-cell RNA-seq, islets were pooled from three Gcg-Cre;ROSAflox/+ mice and three CBP/p300αDKO;ROSAflox/+ mice at 4 weeks of age. Each group contained 300-400 islets, which were digested with 0.25% Trypsin-EDTA (Sigma-Aldrich) for 5 min at 37 ℃. Digestion was terminated with an equal volume of ice-cold RPMI-1640 containing 10% FBS and the sample was centrifuged at 500 g for 3 min. The suspension was then sieved and the pellet was resuspended in ice cold PBS containing 0.2% BSA. Cell viability and number were assessed by Trypan blue staining and the Eve automatic cell counter respectively. Approximately 10,000 - 15,000 cells for each sample were loaded into the 10× Chromium Chip B according to the 10× Genomics Single Cell 30 Reagent Kit v3 GEM protocol. The sequencing strategy used was the Illumina NovaSeq PE150. The scRNAseq data were subsequently processed using Cell Ranger v. 5.0.1 (10× Genomics) to make fastq files for each sample. Cell Ranger Count aligned reads to the mm10 reference genome via STAR. To enable mapping of tdTomato-derived transcripts, the sequence for tdTomato was added to the reference genome and GTF file. Cell filtration was performed with Seurat v4.0.0, removing low quality sequencing data (parameters: nFeature > 200, nUMI > 1000, log10GenesPerUMI > 0.7, mt < 30%, percent of rbc < 0.05) and potential doublets were removed by DoubleFinder69. Count matrices were normalized and scaled using the NormalizeData function with standard parameters. Dimensionality reduction was performed via principal-component analysis (PCA) to enable cell clustering. Cell clustering was done using the FindClusters method with variable-feature 2000 and resolution 0.4. Uniform manifold approximation and projection (u-MAP) was performed. Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA)70 was used to complete Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG term enrichment analysis with the Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB) C5 GO gene sets and C2 KEGG gene sets (version 7.2) separately. Slingshot71 could provide the lineage structure and pseudotime variables inferences for cells along each lineage. The slingshot analysis was performed by slingshot R package (version 1.8.0). Initially, the dimensionally reduced Seurat object was transformed into a SingleCellExperiment object by as.SingleCellExperiment function. Pancreatic α cells from WT mice were selected as a starting cluster for the trajectory inference. Then, FitGAM function in tradeSeq package72 (version 1.4.0) was used to fit the nonlinear function between gene expression and pseudotime using negative binomial generalized additive model (NB-GAM). By using the associationTest function, the top 100 genes whose expression levels significantly differed from pseudotime were chosen to create a heatmap.

To classify hormone-positive and hormone-negative cells, Gcg+ and Gcg- cells were defined using the Pareto density-based cutoff strategy described by Perez-Frances et al73. Normalized Gcg expression values were fitted with Pareto density functions, and cells above the Pareto-derived threshold were classified as Gcg+, whereas those below were classified as Gcg-. The same approach was applied to define tdTomato+ and tdTomato- cells. The cutoff values used for classification were Gcg: 4.384858 and tdTomato: 2.281258.

Transmission electron microscopy

For ultrastructure observation, islets from 3-4 weeks old WT and CBP/p300αDKO mice were immediately hand-picked without filtration after digestion. Each group contained 200 islets. Then the purified islets were chemically fixed with 2.5% glutaraldehyde in phosphate buffer at real temperature for 2 h. After washing, specimens were osmicated with 1% osmium tetraoxide in the same buffer. Then, specimens were washed and dehydrated in ethanol, embedded into Epon 812. After polymerization, 50-100 nm sections were cut and stained. Micrographs were taken by Transmission Electron Microscope (Hitachi, Japan).

Cell culture and treatment

α-TC1-6 cells (a mouse glucagonoma cell line) were cultured in DMEM (Gibco, #10567-014) supplemented with 10% (v/v) FBS, 10 mM HEPES and 100 IU/ml penicillin and 100 mg/ml streptomycin at 37°C in a humidified 5% CO2 atmosphere. Empty plasmids and shRNA interference plasmids targeted Slc7a2 were designed and synthesized from GeneChem (Shanghai, China). Plasmid transfection was carried out by Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. For inhibiting CBP/p300 HAT activity, 3 μM A-485 was used to treat α-TC1-6 cells. After infection or A-485 treatment, cells were harvested for RNA isolation or protein extraction and further analysis. For amino acid starvation and arginine re-stimulation experiments, α-TC1-6 cells were incubated with HBSS buffer containing 1 g/L glucose and 0.2% BSA for 50 min (amino acid starvation) and then treated with 400 μM arginine for 10 min. The target sequences of shRNA plasmids are provided in Supplementary Table 2.

qPCR and Western blotting analysis

For qPCR, total RNA was extracted from α-TC1-6 cells using TRIzol reagent (Vazyme). cDNA was synthesized using a HiScript III 1st Strand cDNA Synthesis Kit (Vazyme). Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) was performed using the ChamQ Universal SYBR qPCR Master Mix (Vazyme). The relative mRNA level of the target gene was calculated using the 2-△△Ct method. The △Ct was computed with normalization to 18s rRNA or beta-actin, which served as the internal control. Primer sequences can be obtained in Supplementary Table 3.

α-TC1-6 cells were treated with RIPA lysis buffer (Aksmics, Shanghai, China) for total protein extraction. Histone was extracted using the EpiQuik Total Histone Extraction Kit (EpiGentek, NY, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Primary antibodies are listed as following: rabbit anti-S6 (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology), rabbit anti-pS6Ser240/244 (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology), rabbit anti-CREB (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology), rabbit anti-pCREB (1:1000; Cell Signaling Technology), mouse anti-HSP90 (1:1000; Santa Cruz Biotechnology). Rabbit anti-H3K9Ac, rabbit anti-H3K18Ac, rabbit anti-H3K27Ac, rabbit anti-H4K12Ac, rabbit anti-H4K8Ac, and rabbit anti-Histone H4 were all purchased from PTM Bio (1:1000 dilution). HSP90 or Histone H4 was used as an internal control to normalize band intensity. Horseradish peroxidase-coupled goat-anti-rabbit IgG or goat-anti-mouse IgG (1:2000; Cell Signaling Technology, USA) were used as a secondary antibody. ## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In new study titled “CBP/p300-Slc7a2 axis is critical for the expansion and maintenance of functional pancreatic α cell mass”, Wang et al. generated tissue-specific knockout mice to examine the importance of histone acetyltransferase p300/CBP in α cells, they meticulously analyzed the phenotype and report new findings. Specifically, they report that α-cell-specific double knockout mice for p300/CBP exhibit hypoglucagonemia and hyperaminoacidemia due to reduced α-cell mass. Furthermore, they explore multiple potential mechanisms and conclude that CBP/p300 is a critical regulator of functional α-cell mass by modulating amino acid sensing via Slc7a2. The research was conducted under a highly rigorous design, yielding robust results. While several concerns are noted below, the overall quality of the study appears exceptionally high.
1. Since the mouse model used Gcg-Cre, Cre recombinase is expected to cause CBP and p300 gene deficiency in Gcg-expressing cells other than α-cells. For example, it should be examined whether there are effects on intestinal L-cells.
2. The discovery that α-cell mass increases during the early juvenile stage from 1 to 2 weeks of age is highly intriguing. Since α-cell mass in CBP/p300αDKO mice is normal at 1 week of age, this suggests that CBP/p300 is dispensable for α-cell development during the fetal period. However, the subsequent impairment in α-cell growth suggests that the physiological increase in α-cell mass during the early postnatal period is a CBP/p300-dependent response, although the driver for this response has not been addressed. Could the physiological increase in α-cell mass during the early postnatal period be explained by a mechanism similar to that observed with GcgR antibody administration?
Minor point
3. Could experiments using the HAT inhibitor A-485 be further examined using mutant CBP and p300 that have lost HAT activity?

### Reviewer 2

Wang et al generated conditional CBP/p300 double KO in alpha-cells on alpha-cell expansion and mass, differentiation and function. Pancreatic alpha-cell-specific deletion of CBP/p300 induced hypoglucagonemia and hyperaminoacidemia, without affecting fasting blood glucose. Alpha-cell CBP/p300 dKO impaired postnatal alpha-cell expansion and differentiation, resulting in decreased alpha-cell mass and to development of hypoglucagonemia. In addition, CBP/p300 deficiency prevented glucagon receptor antibody-stimulated alpha-cell proliferation. Mechanistically, the authors describe a novel CBP/p300-Slc7A2 axis, regulating lysine-induced histone acetylation, including that of the glucagon (Gcg), Mafb and Pcsk2 genes. CBP/p300 KO induces autophagic cell death through attenuation of SLC7A2/arginine-stimulated mTORC1 signaling. Collectively, the authors conclude that in alpha-cells, CBP/p300 are central regulators of alpha-cell mass and function by orchestrating SLC7A2-mediated amino acid sensing. In general, the study design is sound, the findings are interesting, and the manuscript is well-written. However, CBP and p300 are ubiquitous nuclear proteins that play a central role in regulating histone acetyl-transferase activity; therefore, it is not surprising that knocking out both genes impair transcription and cellular growth, differentiation and function. The role of this pathway in regulating alpha-cell function in physiology, e.g. under conditions of amino acid deprivation or overload is not clear. It is also not clear whether this pathway is perturbed in diabetes and/or obesity. New experimental data are required to strengthen the core mechanistic components of the proposed model and to demonstrate its relevance to disease pathophysiology.

1. Are there any alterations in CBP, p300 and/or Slc7a2 expression in alpha-cells in animal models of diabetes and/or obesity/metabolic associated liver dysfuncton(MASLD) and even more important in human subjects? 2. Glucagon deficiency affected amino acids degradation, but not hepatic glucose production, evident by similar fasting glucose, pyruvate tolerance and expression of gluconeogenic enzymes. Are mouse models of glucagon deficiency relevant for studying the role of glucagon in human physiology? Please explain.

### Reviewer 4

Wang et al use Gcg-Cre to delete the histone acetyltransferases p300 and CBP in pancreatic α cells. The KO shows a partial reduction in circulating glucagon and modest increases in several plasma amino acids, which the authors attribute to loss of α cell identity, reduced α cell mass and proliferation, arising from diminished α-cell gene expression. They nominate Slc7a2 as a mediator, and that the reduced Slc7a2 leads to reduced H3K27ac at the Gcg and Mafb loci and their gene downregulation, and a failure to mount α-cell hyperplasia after anti-Gcgr treatment.
The findings on α-cell identity and proliferation overlap with prior Neurog3-Cre genetics showing that p300/CBP are required for islet endocrine cell mass and proliferation. Please cite and discuss this study, since the overlap limits the incremental advance. A significant issue is that most data shown are underpowered, with experiments from Figures 1c, 2, 3, 5, and 6 presented at n = 3 and no justification of sample size.
For the core narrative, the authors argue that loss of p300/CBP downregulates Slc7a2, which then maintains α-cell identity through H3K27ac at Gcg and Mafb, and amino acid-driven proliferation. This interpretation does not fully acknowledge that p300/CBP are fundamental drivers of tissue-specific gene expression that establish endocrine identity. It is therefore equally plausible that Slc7a2 downregulation is a downstream consequence of identity erosion rather than the primary cause. To support causality, one would need in vivo evidence that Slc7a2 loss is sufficient to reduce H3K27ac at Gcg and Mafb with concordant transcriptional downregulation. A recent Slc7a2-/- report does not show loss of α-cell identity. For proliferation, α cells lacking p300/CBP already show impaired proliferation, so the lack of an amino acid response may reflect a general failure to traverse the cell cycle, in addition to any defect in amino acid sensing.

1. The Gcg-Cre driver is active in pancreatic α cells, intestinal L cells, and preproglucagon neurons. Did p300/CBP loss in gut and brain influence oral glucose tolerance or energy metabolism?
2. Did the authors measure glucagon secretion from intact islets, and is insulin secretion altered in vivo or ex vivo?
3. For Figures 2b and 3c, please report absolute values in addition to fold change.

Joint integration followed by trajectory inference is a standard way to place both genotypes on the same manifold so that differences can be attributed to biology.

We sincerely thank the reviewers for their constructive and insightful comments on our manuscript entitled “CBP/p300-Slc7a2 axis is critical for the expansion and maintenance of functional pancreatic α cell mass”. In response, we have carefully addressed each point raised and incorporated new experimental data and expanded discussion where appropriate. These revisions have strengthened the manuscript. Below, we provide a detailed point-by-point response to all comments. Newly added data are included in the revised figures and text as indicated.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):

Response: We appreciate your constructive comment. We fully agree that potential off-target effects of Gcg-Cre in intestinal L-cells should be evaluated to ensure that the observed phenotypes are primarily α-cell specific. To address this issue, we performed additional experiments. Intestinal co-expression of GLP-1 and the tdTomato in Gcg-Cre-driven tdTomato lineage-tracing WT and CBP/p300αDKO mice confirmed that Gcg-Cre was indeed active in the intestinal L-cells (Extended Data Fig.1a). 2. The discovery that α-cell mass increases during the early juvenile stage from 1 to 2 weeks of age is highly intriguing. Since α-cell mass in CBP/p300αDKO mice is normal at 1 week of age, this suggests that CBP/p300 is dispensable for α-cell development during the fetal period. Could the physiological increase in α-cell mass during the early postnatal period be explained by a mechanism similar to that observed with GcgR antibody administration?
Response: We appreciate your insightful suggestion. In various models of GCGR blockade, elevating circulating amino acids have been identified as key secretory signals that drive excessive α-cell proliferation through mTOR-dependent pathways [2,3,4]. Notably, Solloway et al. [5] reported that nearly all proteinogenic amino acids and ornithine are markedly elevated in neonatal Gcgr+/+ mice (P7–P14), with levels progressively decreasing toward adulthood. This decline coincides with the cessation of postnatal α-cell proliferation in wild-type animals. Consistently, Bozadjieva et al. [6] showed that mTORC1 signaling was essential for α cell–mass maintenance during the nutritional transition from a milk-based to a chow-based diet, as α cell-specific mTORC1 regulator Raptor (αRaptorKO) knockout mice exhibited impaired α-cell expansion during this period. Taken together, these findings support the idea that early postnatal increase in α-cell mass is driven by elevated serum amino acids and activation of the mTORC1 pathway during lactation.

Although glucagon is well known for its rapid glucose-elevating action and clinical use in treating severe hypoglycemia, we did not observe decreased fasting glucose level in CBP/p300αDKO mice despite their hypoglucagonemia. Similar findings have been reported in other models: (i) α-cell ablation using diphtheria toxin in embryos or adult mice minimally affects fasting glucose [11-13], and (ii) Gcg knockout mice also maintain normal fasting glucose levels [14]. These findings suggest that basal hepatic glucose production can be preserved through residual glucagon secretion and compensatory mechanisms that maintain glucose homeostasis. In contrast, amino acid dysregulation is a highly penetrant and conserved hallmark of glucagon deficiency. Elevated circulating amino acid levels have been consistently observed in Gcg knockout, Gcgr knockout, and GCGR antibody blockade mouse models [15]. Li Hong et al. reported a patient with a homozygous GCGR c.958_960del (p.Phe320del) variant who exhibited normal blood glucose level, but persistent hyperaminoacidemia [16]. Patients undergoing pancreatectomy likewise develop severe hyperaminoacidemia that can be alleviated by glucagon administration, whereas individuals with glucagon-producing tumors exhibit profound hypoaminoacidemia [17]. A practical extension of this conserved biology is that plasma amino acid concentrations are now used clinically as pharmacodynamic readouts of GCGR activity in trials of dual (glucagon/GLP-1) or triple (glucagon/GLP-1/GIP) receptor agonists [18].
